entry.title: Inside Alacritty: How a GPU-Accelerated Terminal Emulator Renders Your Shell

link.title: Inside Alacritty: How a GPU-Accelerated Terminal Emulator Renders Your Shell

entry.content:
Open a half-gigabyte log file with cat in a typical terminal and the interface starts to melt: keystrokes echo late, the scrollbar fights back, and a CPU core saturates. Run the same command in Alacritty and it stays smooth. The difference is not shell trickery or clever output buffering — it is an architectural decision made in 2017 and refined since: keep terminal state on the CPU, but let the GPU composite every frame.

“GPU-accelerated terminal” sounds like marketing, so it is worth pinning down what it actually means. A terminal’s job is to turn program bytes into a grid of styled characters, then put that grid on screen. Most of the cost is bookkeeping: parsing escape sequences, maintaining scrollback, and redrawing the visible slice. When that bookkeeping is paired with a renderer that uploads rasterized glyphs once into a GPU texture and afterwards only pushes a few thousand textured quads per frame, the parser and the paint loop stop competing for the same resources. Everything in Alacritty’s design follows from that separation.

Between the moment your shell writes a byte to the pseudoterminal and the moment a pixel lights up, the data crosses five stages: PTY read, escape-sequence parsing, grid mutation, damage collection, and GPU draw. This article walks each stage through Alacritty’s actual source on master — every symbol and line number below links into the upstream repo at the version current when written (binary crate 0.18.0-dev). It is all Rust, using the 2024 edition with a toolchain floor of 1.85.

Alacritty's data flow: the binary crate wires windows and input; a dedicated "PTY reader" thread parses shell bytes into the shared Term; the grid stores cells; the renderer turns damaged cells into GPU draws. Click any node to open the file on GitHub.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Two crates, one screen. The workspace holds four members members, L2: the GUI binary, the window-free alacritty_terminal library, and two config helper crates. The library gates its tty and event_loop modules off for wasm targets wasm gates, L8, which is why its terminal logic can be tested headlessly against recorded byte streams.
  • The main thread owns windows, not I/O. Startup builds a winit event loop whose user events are Alacritty’s own Event type EventLoop::with_user_event, L138, then one WindowContext per window creates the shell’s PTY tty::new, L201 and spawns the I/O thread event_loop.spawn, L227.
  • Bytes are parsed straight into state. pty_read leases the shared FairMutex, reads chunks from the PTY, and calls parser.advance to mutate Term in place pty_read, L103, parser.advance, L153.
  • One Wakeup per burst. After a parse burst the loop sends a single Event::Wakeup Wakeup, L166 instead of one per write — so a fast prompt like Starship redrawing on every command coalesces into one frame.
  • The grid is a ring buffer. Scrollback rotates by moving an index, not memory Storage, L33.
  • Damage before pixels. Display::draw pulls per-line damage damage(), L458 and merges it into the frame’s DamageTracker before any GL call Display::draw, L775.
  • Two shader backends. GLSL3 versus GLES2 is chosen at startup from the context’s shader version backend selection, L146 — the same “detect the hardware, pick the cheapest correct path” philosophy that tools like ripgrep apply to CPU work.

A closer cut: the I/O loop's read and write paths around the FairMutex, Term's escape-sequence handler callbacks, the ring-buffer Storage, and the renderer's backend selection feeding the glyph atlas.

The Workspace: a Library That Happens to Ship a GUI

The first thing worth understanding is the crate boundary. alacritty_terminal contains the entire terminal state machine — grid, cells, scrollback, selection, vi-mode cursor — with zero knowledge of windows, GPUs, or keyboard events. The alacritty binary crate then adds the platform layers: winit for windows, glutin for the OpenGL context glutin, L31, crossfont for rasterizing fonts, and an input Processor Processor, L77 that maps key and mouse events onto bindings or PTY writes.

That boundary pays off twice. First, the library ships reference tests that replay raw byte recordings into a Term and diff the resulting grid snapshot — dozens of .recording plus grid.json pairs live under alacritty_terminal/tests/ref/, covering VT cases from tab stops to 24-bit color. Second, the state machine cannot drift toward UI concerns: if a feature needs a window, it must live in the binary crate and talk to the library through the event proxy — EventProxy wraps a winit EventLoopProxy and implements the library’s EventListener trait EventProxy, L2072.

Stage One: Shell Bytes Become Terminal State

A pseudoterminal (PTY) is a kernel object: the shell runs on the slave side while the emulator holds the master, reading bytes programs print and writing bytes you type. On Unix the master is an openpty with a child-exit watcher unix Pty, L102; on Windows the same trait set is implemented over ConPTY ConPTY, L110. Both backends expose EventedReadWrite, so either can be polled without busy-waiting.

The I/O thread’s heart is EventLoop::pty_read pty_read, L103. Its speed trick is a lock protocol: the thread first leases the terminal lock lease, L116 and only escalates to a blocking lock when its read buffer is full try_lock, L139. The renderer holds the same FairMutex only for the microseconds it takes to snapshot cells. Under a cat flood, the parser can churn through megabytes while the UI thread still wins the lock regularly — the reason the interface stays responsive.

Parsing itself is delegated to the external vte crate, re-exported from the library root pub use vte, L23. Term implements the Handler trait for every escape family impl Handler, L1059: cursor moves, SGR color changes, scrolling regions, insert and delete lines. The parser never allocates strings it doesn’t need; it just drives those callbacks over the incoming bytes.

Output to the shell flows the other way through a Notifier Notifier, L333, which funnels the terminal-side Event enum Event enum, L14 — PtyWrite, Resize, Shutdown — into the I/O loop’s channel, where pty_write drains it toward the PTY. The terminal pushes UI-relevant events like title changes through its event proxy; grid changes wake the renderer once per burst.

The Grid: Scrollback as a Ring Buffer

Everything the handler mutates lands in a Grid<Cell> Grid, L110: a cursor, a display_offset for how far you’ve scrolled back, and the raw rows. Term actually holds two grids — the primary screen and the alternate screen Term, L268 — because that is how full-screen TUI programs work. When fzf takes over your terminal, it activates the alternate grid Term struct grids, L281; when it exits, the primary grid — and your scrollback — reappears untouched.

The storage behind the grid is the quiet highlight. Naive scrolling memmoves thousands of rows; Alacritty’s Storage<T> Storage, L33 instead keeps rows in a plain Vec<Row<T>> plus a zero field marking which element is currently the bottommost line zero field, L41. Rotation becomes a modular index update — the comments call it out explicitly against slice::rotate_left’s memory rearrangement rotate doc, L17 — and shrinking scrollback only trims the logical length, deferring reallocation. Each row is a fixed-width Row<T> Row, L17.

Each Cell is deliberately tiny: a char, foreground and background colors, and a Flags bitmask Cell, L141 packed as u16 bitflags Flags, L22. Wide characters, zerowidth marks, hyperlinks, and underline colors are rare, so they hide behind an Option<Arc<CellExtra>> — the common cell stays flat, and grids copy cheaply. Scrollback defaults to 10,000 lines scrolling_history, L359, adjustable from config.

Finally, mutation and rendering communicate through damage. Term accumulates a TermDamageState: a “fully damaged” flag plus per-line (left, right) column ranges. damage() damage(), L458 hands those out — always adding both the old and new cursor positions — and reset_damage() reset_damage(), L489 clears the slate. A fast full-screen rewrite marks everything; a single printed character damages one line segment.

Stage Two: Damage-Aware GPU Rendering

Display Display, L342 owns the OpenGL context, the glyph cache, and the DamageTracker DamageTracker, L16. Each draw() begins by snapshotting RenderableContent RenderableContent, L27 — the visible slice of the grid resolved into RenderableCell values with final colors RenderableCell, L189 — then merges the terminal’s damage into the frame tracker, plus UI overlays like search or the visual bell. A telling detail: the Term lock is dropped before any GL work drop lock, L815, so parsing resumes while the frame is being built.

Which shader backend runs is decided once at context creation: GLSL3 when the context offers shader version 3.3 or newer on desktop GL, GLES2 otherwise backend selection, L146, overridable from config. Both implement the same TextRenderer trait TextRenderer, L48; the difference is subpixel antialiasing, which the GLES2 path must split across three shader passes.

Text is drawn as textured quads over one GPU resource: the glyph atlas Atlas, L33. It is a square RGBA texture where glyphs are packed row by row, tracking row_extent, row_baseline, and row_tallest as the allocator state. Atlas::insert Atlas::insert, L119 either fits the glyph or returns Full/GlyphTooLarge AtlasInsertError, L64, and the cache above it rasterizes on demand GlyphCache, L46 — first use of a glyph costs a CPU rasterization; every later frame is just a texture lookup. Cells are batched by atlas texture; a batch flushes when the texture changes or the batch fills batch flush, L119, keeping draw calls low on dense output. Underlines, strikes, and the cursor are layered on afterward as rectangle geometry cursor rects, L896.

From Cargo Build to First Prompt

The fastest path is cargo install alacritty — platform libraries still apply. From a source checkout, the build is cargo build --release cargo build –release, L242, producing target/release/alacritty binary path, L256. The release profile enables thin LTO.

System dependencies are the usual suspects for GUI code in Rust: on Debian/Ubuntu, cmake g++ pkg-config libfontconfig1-dev libxcb-xfixes0-dev libxkbcommon-dev python3 deps, L86; on Windows, the MSVC toolchain plus Clang 3.9 or newer Windows, L229. On Linux/BSD the windowing backends are compile-time features — default ["wayland", "x11"] default features, L88 — and you can force just one with --no-default-features --features=wayland (or x11) feature flags, L250. On macOS, make app produces an app bundle, with make app-universal for an x86+ARM binary.

Two post-build steps complete the setup: installing the terminfo entry with sudo tic -xe alacritty,alacritty-direct extra/alacritty.info terminfo, L298 so programs emit sequences Alacritty understands, and dropping the binary onto your PATH. Launch it and the WindowContext machinery from the first diagram runs: PTY spawned, I/O thread started, the first Wakeup turns into your prompt.

Honest Limits

  • No tabs, no splits — by design. The README FAQ states plainly that you won’t find “tabs or splits (which are best left to a window manager or terminal multiplexer)” nor a GUI config editor tabs FAQ, L104. Multiplexing is delegated to tools like tmux.
  • “GPU-accelerated” is not a benchmark claim. The README itself says throughput is quantified with vtebench while latency and frame consistency are “more difficult to quantify,” and that some terminals intentionally slow down to save resources — test your own workloads vtebench, L86.
  • OpenGL only. Rendering sits on glutin with EGL/WGL and two GL shader backends; there is no wgpu or Vulkan backend in this tree glutin, L31.
  • Version state. The checkout behind this article is 0.18.0-dev, an unreleased development snapshot, so cited line numbers will drift as development continues.
entry.summary: A source-code tour of Alacritty's architecture: the PTY event loop, the grid ring buffer, ANSI parsing, damage tracking, and the OpenGL glyph atlas that draws your shell.

entry.title: Inside fd: How the Fast Rust Find Replacement Walks Your Filesystem

link.title: Inside fd: How the Fast Rust Find Replacement Walks Your Filesystem

entry.content:
Every developer knows the ritual: you want the file named foo, and out comes find . -iname "*foo*" -not -path "*/node_modules/*". Quotes because find’s argument order is a trap, -iname because you do not remember the casing, and a -not -path filter because find happily descends into directories you told git to forget. Then you run fd foo — no quotes, no flags — and the answers scroll by instantly, case-insensitively, already skipping everything your .gitignore covers. The difference is not cosmetic; it is architectural.

What actually happens in the milliseconds between pressing Enter and the first path appearing? Most people imagine a single loop: walk the tree, test each name against the pattern, print. fd’s real answer is a small distributed system: a clap-derived option parser, a smart-case decision, a compiled matcher, a configurable WalkBuilder, a pool of worker threads pushing batches through a bounded channel, and a receiver thread that silently chooses between “sort everything” and “stream now” modes.

This post walks fd’s actual source (v10.5.2, the master branch) to explain how each stage works and why the stages are ordered the way they are. If you have read our ripgrep deep dive, some of the machinery will look familiar — fd borrows the same ignore crate that powers ripgrep’s walker, and the borrowing is explicit in the code.

Overview: fd splits into a CLI layer, a matcher builder, the parallel walk core, shared data types, and the printing stage. One bounded channel connects walkers to the receiver.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Startup is a single function: run, L83 parses Opts, L39 via clap derive, translates flags into one immutable Config, L14, and ends by calling walk::scan — fd has no long-lived state between these stages.
  • Pattern mode is decided up front by determine_pattern_type, L226: regex by default, --glob, --exact, or --fixed-strings; the same routine also powers smart case at L106, where a pattern containing any uppercase character silently re-enables case sensitivity.
  • build_patterns, L73 compiles your strings once into a RegexSet, a GlobSet, or the trivial MatchAll; for multiple --and patterns a name must satisfy every regex, enforced by the count check at L30.
  • build_walker, L345 is where speed policy lives: hidden files, ignore rules, depth limits, symlink handling and the thread count are wired into ignore’s WalkBuilder, finishing with build_parallel() at L400.
  • spawn_senders, L441 registers one filtering closure per worker thread; results are grouped into pointer-sized BatchSender, L73 batches so the channel moves Arc<Mutex<Vec>> handles rather than one message per entry.
  • Backpressure is a single line: bounded(2 * config.threads), L621. When the receiver falls behind, the channel fills and the walker threads simply block — no unbounded memory growth on huge trees.
  • The receiver is a ReceiverBuffer, L128 that waits on recv_deadline, L186: if 100 ms pass without completion it flips to streaming, and if the walk finished inside the window, stop, L280 sorts the buffer first.
  • Thread count defaults to default_num_threads, L804 — available_parallelism() capped at 64 so fd does not spawn 128 threads on a big build server for a search that finishes in 20 ms.

Detail view: the startup stages on the left feed the walk core; the filter closure in the middle orders checks from cheapest to most expensive before anything is sent across the channel.

From Cargo Build to First Search

fd is a single small crate, which makes the build story unusually legible. The package is named fd-find (Cargo.toml, L16) while the binary it installs is fd (L29) — that split is why the install command is cargo install fd-find even though you type fd afterwards. The crate targets edition 2024 and requires Rust 1.90.0 (L20), so a current stable toolchain (see our Rust tour) is enough: cargo build --release produces the binary directly, or cargo build for a fast debug build that only records line tables for dependencies.

The release profile is tuned for a CLI tool: lto = true, strip = true, codegen-units = 1 (L90) — smaller binary, fewer jumps, no symbol table for a tool whose entire job is to start fast. Feature flags matter too: the default set is ["use-jemalloc", "completions"] (L95), and use-jemalloc swaps in the tikv-jemallocator global allocator, but only behind a long cfg gate in main.rs, L48 that excludes Windows, macOS, Android and a few embedded targets — macOS is disabled on purpose due to a jemalloc bug (Cargo.toml, L66). A base feature exists for packagers who want just the allocator. The heavy lifting comes from the dependency list: ignore = "0.4.28" (L37), crossbeam-channel (L45), regex, globset and memchr — the same BurntSushi crates you would find under the hood of ripgrep, which is no coincidence given the shared flag heritage documented in cli.rs, L109.

The Parallel Walk: One WalkBuilder, N Threads

The heart is ignore::WalkParallel. scan, L602 opens the channel, then spawns the receiver and lets walker.run(...) occupy the remaining threads. There is no manual work distribution: WalkParallel hands each thread directory entries as it discovers them, and every thread runs the same closure built inside spawn_senders, L441. Two atomic flags — quit_flag and interrupt_flag (WorkerState, L304) — let a Ctrl-C handler or an early exit (a --quiet match, a full --max-results quota) tell every worker to return WalkState::Quit on its next entry (L458).

The closure’s first lines are micro-decisions that add up. The depth-0 root entry is skipped (L478) so fd lists contents, not the directory itself. A --ignore-contain check tests for sentinel files before any other work, explicitly to save syscalls (L462). And when the walker hands over an Err for a broken symlink, fd does not give up: broken_symlink_from_err, L643 unwraps the error chain, confirms the target was a symlink via symlink_metadata, and rebuilds it into a printable entry — so broken links still show up in results.

Filtering: Cheap Checks Before Expensive Syscalls

The worker closure is essentially an ordered gauntlet, and the order is the optimization. First patterns.matches_path, L507 tests the file name against the compiled matcher — pure CPU, zero syscalls, so most junk entries are rejected before the OS is ever asked a question. Only then come the filters that need metadata, each gated behind an Option so a search without -e, -t, -S or --changed-within pays nothing for them.

The extension filter checks entry_path.file_name() against a RegexSet of patterns like \.rs$, built once during startup (main.rs, L330, case-insensitive). File-type selection delegates to FileTypes::should_ignore, L50, which implements -t d/f/l/x/e/s. Owner (Unix-only) comes next, then size, where SizeFilter::is_within, L69 compares against +500m/-2g-style bounds parsed with SI and binary prefixes at startup (L35). Time filters run last before output: TimeFilter::applies_to, L57 accepts durations (2h), dates, or @epoch seconds, and all supplied constraints must pass. Crucially, the metadata each of these needs is not fetched repeatedly: DirEntry caches it in a OnceCell (dir_entry.rs, L91), so a size filter followed by a time filter costs one stat, not two. A surviving entry is colored in the worker thread (L578) — even LS_COLORS styling is moved off the single receiver.

.gitignore Rules and –unrestricted

The reason fd “just works” in a repository is that build_walker configures the ignore crate to interpret git’s own ignore machinery: .git_ignore, .git_global, .git_exclude (walk.rs, L355) plus parent-directory rules — the same semantics git uses when deciding what to commit, which our git internals tour covers from git’s side. One subtlety is require_git: by default fd only honors .gitignore files when it is inside an actual git repository (L358), a deliberate choice to avoid surprising ignore behavior in plain folders. fd adds two custom layers git does not have: .fdignore registered via add_custom_ignore_filename (L366) and a global ignore file at ~/.config/fd/ignore (L369).

All of it is switchable. --no-ignore (-I) disables the ignore stack, and -u/--unrestricted (cli.rs, L137) is a single-keystroke alias for --no-ignore --hidden, mirroring ripgrep’s -u. The --exclude globs are implemented separately from ignore files, as a gitignore-style Override built with a ! prefix per pattern (build_overrides, L328) — so excludes compose with, rather than replace, repository rules.

The 100 Milliseconds That Sort Your Results

Printing has a hidden decision you never see. The receiver starts in Buffering mode (ReceiverMode, L26) and accumulates entries up to MAX_BUFFER_LENGTH = 1000 (L123). Each recv call carries a deadline of 100 ms (DEFAULT_MAX_BUFFER_TIME, L125); if the deadline fires first, the mode flips to Streaming and the buffer is dumped unsorted — for a huge tree you get results immediately, sorted-ness be damned. But if the entire walk completes inside the window, stop() sorts the buffer before printing (L282). That is why small searches come out alphabetically ordered and multi-second ones do not: fd bets that most searches finish faster than a human notices, and pays sorting only when it is free.

Everything downstream is also batch- and lock-aware. receive wraps stdout in a BufWriter (L433), flushes opportunistically when the channel runs dry, and print_entry, L17 handles hyperlinks, colors, custom separators and --format templates. For --exec, the receiving side changes shape entirely: with per-result execution fd clones the receiver onto every thread (L414) and the sender drops its batch size to 1 (L447) to spread commands evenly, while batch-mode --exec keeps big batches.

Honest Limits

fd is a filename finder, and it does not pretend otherwise. Nothing in src/ reads file contents — there is no content-search module — so greping inside files is out of scope by design; pair fd with a content tool, which is exactly the division of labor between fd and ripgrep. Consequences follow from that scope: a pattern containing / cannot match a bare file name, so fd raises a friendly error suggesting --full-path instead of silently returning nothing (main.rs, L176).

Default behavior has sharp edges worth knowing. Ignore rules apply only inside git repositories unless you pass --no-require-git (cli.rs, L96); hidden files mean only leading-dot names (cli.rs, L40) — macOS’s resource forks or Windows system attributes are not “hidden” to fd; and smart case is evaluated per-pattern, with fixed/exact strings falling back to a plain uppercase scan (patterns.rs, L118). Platform quirks are documented in the tree: --list-details shells out to ls and errors on Windows without GNU ls installed (main.rs, L453), and the jemalloc allocator is compiled out on macOS and Windows entirely (Cargo.toml, L66). None of these are bugs — they are the cost of the single-crate, do-one-thing design that makes the source above worth reading in an afternoon.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of fd: how the ignore crate's parallel WalkBuilder, a cheap-first filter chain, gitignore handling and a 100 ms output buffer make fd so fast.

entry.title: Inside the fish Shell: How Typed Characters Become Running Jobs

link.title: Inside the fish Shell: How Typed Characters Become Running Jobs

entry.content:
Open fish for the first time, type git che, and a gray ghost of a full command appears at the end of your line — a real suggestion pulled from your history, not a canned prefix. Press the right-arrow key and it lands in your buffer. No plugin manager, no ~/.fishrc incantation, no four-hour rabbit hole. That “it just works” feeling is the surface of a very deep machine, and the machine is worth opening.

The moment you press Enter, that friendly line editor transforms into something closer to a compiler backend: the buffer is tokenized, parsed into a typed tree, expanded through five distinct stages, packaged into a Job of Process structs, assigned a process group, and handed to posix_spawn or fork. A piped command like grep error log/**.log | wc -l is not “run” — it is assembled, piece by piece, from data structures fish has been mutating since before you finished typing.

One more reason this tour is timely: fish was famously a C++ codebase for two decades, but fish 4.0 ported the core to Rust (the changelog tracks it as issue #9512). Today’s master contains no C++ sources at all — just Rust crates, a workspace Cargo.toml declaring version 4.9.3, and the Rust 1.85 MSRV. Reading the source now means reading Rust.

The whole journey at a glance: the interactive reader on the left feeds the parser, expansion turns strings into candidates, and the execution layer turns the AST into real processes — all backed by layered shell state.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Startup is tiny. The binary entry point main, L349 parses flags, decides whether the session is interactive, and calls reader_read, L549 on stdin. Everything users associate with fish — prompt, suggestions, colors — hangs off that single call.
  • The reader parses while you type, not just after Enter. read_i builds a config with syntax_check_ok: true (read_i, L824), so the buffer is continuously parsed for live highlighting and error marking — the dashed edge from the reader back into the parse tree in the diagram.
  • One parse function serves everything. Interactive evaluation, fish -c, config files, and even the highlighter all funnel through parse_source, L257, which calls ast::parse, L1400 to build a JobList tree and wraps it in a ParsedSource, L109 that keeps the original string alive for source ranges.
  • Expansion is a stage machine, not a regex soup. expand_string, L201 drives separate stages for tilde, variables, braces, command substitution, and wildcards — each stage can multiply the candidate list.
  • A Job is built before anything runs. run_1_job, L1546 creates the job object (Job::new, L1665) and only then calls exec_job, L1695. Construction and execution are cleanly separated.
  • Process groups are a first-class concept. Every job carries a JobGroup, L59 holding the pgid, terminal-ownership flags, and a cancel signal — this is what makes Ctrl-C hit the whole piped command and not fish itself.
  • Universal state sits at the bottom of the stack. EnvStack, L212 layers variable scopes; the EnvUniversal, L41 database feeds the universal layer, which is why set -U survives restarts and crosses fish instances.

The detail view: each group in the overview unpacks into the real modules — the readline event loop, the parse tree, the five expansion stages, the spawn path, and the state stores.

Tokenize, Parse, and the Rust AST

Fish’s grammar is unusual among shells because it is typed rather than ad hoc, and the Rust rewrite doubled down on that. The Tokenizer, L238 first turns raw source into a flat stream of TokenType, L18 values — strings, pipes, redirections, ends — handling quoting and escape rules that date back two decades.

Then the interesting part happens. Instead of an interpreter wandering over tokens, ast::parse, L1400 runs a Populator that directly fills Rust structs: a JobPipeline, L767 is one chain of piped commands, AndorJob, L1007 captures and/or chaining, and a DecoratedStatement, L954 is one command with its sudo-style decorators. The result is a strongly-typed tree rooted at JobList (Ast, L1445) — there is no void * node soup, so the compiler itself rejects malformed tree walks.

The Parser, L390 then does evaluation. Its eval_with, L524 parses the string and hands the tree to eval_node, L630, which constructs an ExecutionContext, L119 and dispatches: job lists to run_job_list, L1795, if/while/for to their dedicated run_* methods. Syntax errors are therefore impossible past this point — the doc comment on eval_parsed_source, L561 says exactly that: “Because the source has been parsed, a syntax error is impossible.”

Expansion: Five Stages Before Anything Runs

A fish argument like ~/$project/*.{rs,toml} is not a string — it is a plan that explodes into dozens of real arguments. The expansion layer implements that plan as an ordered stage machine inside expand.rs: stage_cmdsubst, L1389, stage_variables, L1436, stage_braces, L1476, home-directory expansion at stage_home_and_self, L1480, and finally stage_wildcards, L1497.

The stages are honest about their jobs. expand_tilde, L348 consults the environment for $HOME and ~user. expand_variables, L608 implements fish’s signature list semantics — one variable can expand to many arguments, with slices like $list[1..3]. expand_braces, L845 does the Cartesian product. Command substitution (expand_cmdsubst, L969) is special because it must execute code, so it calls into the execution layer — you can see the edge from expansion to exec_subshell_for_expand in the detail diagram.

Wildcards get their own module because they are the only stage that touches the filesystem. wildcard_expand_string, L1021 walks directory trees to materialize matches for * and the recursive **, while wildcard_match, L1078 does the filtering and wildcard_has, L1165 decides whether a string is a glob at all. If you like this layer, the fast path-friendly sibling tool in this series — ripgrep for searching — solves adjacent problems with the same rigor.

From a Job to a Living Process

Execution begins as bookkeeping. run_1_job, L1546 checks --no-execute, records the executing node for profiling, and applies per-job variable assignments before Job::new, L1665 assembles a Job, L613 — a sequence of Process, L365 structs, each tagged with a ProcessType, L55 of external, builtin, function, or block. Only when the whole job is described does exec_job, L86 start it.

exec_job is where the pipe plumbing lives. Its comment explains that up to three pipes can be “in flight” — the one to read from, the one to write to, and the one for the next process — and the loop over processes wires them up, passing each to exec_process_in_job, L1222. That dispatcher routes to exec_builtin_process, L1187 for builtins and exec_block_or_func_process, L1054 for functions, both of which run inside the fish process, recursively re-entering the parser.

External commands take the spawn path. exec_external_command, L861 builds argv/envv, computes a PgroupPolicy (lead a new group, join the job’s pgid, or inherit fish’s), and prefers posix_spawn via PosixSpawner, L96 because it is faster than fork on systems like macOS; otherwise fork_child_for_process, L692 takes over. Meanwhile the JobGroup, L59 tracks whether the job wants the terminal and who is foreground, so job control — suspending, resuming, Ctrl-C — behaves. Finished jobs are collected by job_reap, L983, and wait waits through proc_wait_any, L1115. The pairing of a shell with a fast terminal emulator — alacritty, for instance — only matters because fish is this careful about who owns the tty.

The Reader: Autosuggestions and Highlighting

The interactive layer is the part you actually see. The event loop is Reader::readline, L2570: it consumes CharEvents, applies key bindings resolved through BindingSet, L298, and repaints the screen. Every edit triggers update_autosuggestion, L5591, which asks the persistent History, L1191 store for a matching prefix and then validates it — autosuggest_validate_from_history, L355 re-runs the suggestion through the highlighter to avoid proposing commands that would fail. Pressing right-arrow calls accept_autosuggestion, L5670. Tab completions flow from complete, L2534 into the Pager, L90, and the coloring itself is produced by highlight_shell, L96, which is why invalid commands turn red before you press Enter. If you enjoy that interactive-selection workflow, fzf composes beautifully with fish’s history pager, and starship plugs into the same prompt-event hook fish exposes.

Universal Variables: State That Follows You

set -U EDITOR vim works across every open fish and every future fish. The keeper of that promise is EnvUniversal, L41, which tracks modified keys in a dirty set and writes them via sync, L162 to a single file resolved by default_vars_path, L627 — the fish_variables file in your config directory. Cross-instance awareness comes from a small family of notifier backends; on Linux the notifyd-based NotifydNotifier, L28 watches that file so a second fish session picks up changes without polling. Exported universal variables additionally bump an export generation count, visible right in the struct’s fields.

From Cargo Build to First Prompt

Building fish from source is a standard Rust workflow wrapped in a thin CMake shell, and the README, L116 states the requirements plainly: Rust 1.85 or later with cargo, CMake 3.15+, a C compiler for feature detection, and a network connection since dependencies download automatically. The canonical install path (README, L140) is:

mkdir build; cd build
cmake ..
cmake --build .
sudo cmake --install .

CMake exists because fish needs system feature detection, but underneath it drives cargo: the workspace root Cargo.toml declares the fish binary at src/bin/fish.rs, alongside fish_indent and fish_key_reader, and pins the workspace to edition 2024. The compiled binary needs no runtime interpreter — the AST machinery above is compiled in.

Honest Limits

Fish’s friendliness is a deliberate trade, documented rather than hidden. The design document lists POSIX conformance only as its third goal, to be followed “whenever possible without breaking the above goals” (design.rst, L10), and the bash-migration doc opens with the blunter sentence: “fish is intentionally not POSIX-compatible” (fish_for_bash_users.rst, L4). Practically: variables never word-split, there are no heredocs, string manipulation replaces ${foo%bar}, and only * and ** are glob syntax — a non-matching glob fails the command rather than passing a literal * (fish_for_bash_users.rst, L114). Scripts written for sh/bash need porting; fish is not a drop-in /bin/sh replacement. The Rust port is real but young by shell standards — the C++ era left twenty years of optimization history, and the port notes in the changelog are candid that packaging and build dependencies changed wholesale. None of this is instability so much as a stated identity: fish optimizes for the interactive human first, and the source makes that choice visible at every layer.
entry.summary: A source tour of the fish shell's Rust rewrite: the parser, expansion stages, job groups, universal variables, and the reader that make fish feel magic.

entry.title: Inside fzf: The Fuzzy Matching Architecture Behind Instant Interactive Search

link.title: Inside fzf: The Fuzzy Matching Architecture Behind Instant Interactive Search

entry.content:
Type three characters into fzf while a million lines stream through it, and the best match appears before your finger leaves the key. That is not a shortcut: every keystroke triggers a full pass over every candidate, scoring each one against the query. A typical shell history of 100,000 entries, or a recursive file walk over half a million paths, gets re-ranked from scratch, repeatedly, at human typing speed. Most tools fake this by throttling input or building indexes up front; fzf does neither.

The trick is that nothing in the design is slow enough to need faking. Input arrives in fixed-size chunks that can be matched independently, matching is spread across every CPU core, each core reuses pre-allocated memory arenas so the garbage collector never stalls the loop, and the final ranking compresses into a single 64-bit integer comparison per item. The result is a flow with no stage slower than the one before it, so the perceived latency is just the sum of a few cheap passes.

So what actually happens between the moment fzf starts and the instant the first keystroke produces a ranked list? In this post we walk the Go source of junegunn/fzf and trace the whole journey: the concurrent reader, the chunked store, the scoring algorithm behind the fuzziness, the parallel matcher, and the terminal loop that ties it together. The two diagrams below are generated directly from the repository tree.

The fzf architecture as five collaborating components. Everything left of the matcher runs continuously in the background; everything right of it reacts to your keystrokes. Click any node to open the exact source file on GitHub.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything is coordinated through one event box. The entire runtime is documented in a comment block: the reader pushes EvtReadNew, the terminal pushes EvtSearchNew, the matcher answers with EvtSearchProgress and EvtSearchFin — see core.go, L16. The coordinator wakes, reacts, and then sleeps on a back-off that grows from 10 ms to a 100 ms ceiling, which is how bursts of keystrokes get batched into fewer searches — core.go, L635.
  • The reader never blocks matching. Run spawns the reader and matcher as bare goroutines around a mutex-guarded chunk list: core.go, L204 wires the reader’s pusher straight into ChunkList.Push, core.go, L210 starts ingestion, and core.go, L360 starts the matcher loop before the terminal even exists.
  • Input is chopped into fixed 1024-item chunks. A Chunk is literally a [chunkSize]Item array — constants.go, L40 and chunklist.go, L6. Fixed size is what makes per-chunk caching and work-stealing matching possible later; variable-length lists would break both.
  • Reader→matcher feedback is a CAS on one int. The reader’s poller loop does a compare-and-swap from EvtReadNew to EvtReady before broadcasting into the shared EventBox, and backs its poll interval off from 10 ms toward 50 ms while the stream is quiet — reader.go, L51. No channel storms while a slow command dribbles out bytes.
  • Matching is per-chunk, per-CPU. The matcher sizes its worker pool to runtime.NumCPU() — matcher.go, L61 — and each worker steals chunks off an atomic counter, so adding a core linearly scales the scan — matcher.go, L194.
  • Scores become one machine word. A Result packs the item plus four uint16 ranking slots — result.go, L27 — and on x86 the comparison casts those slots into a single uint64 equality check — result_x86.go, L7. Sorting a million items is then just an O(n) radix pass — result.go, L354.
  • The terminal loop is the only renderer. Keystrokes, repaints, the spinner and the previewer all funnel through a priority-sorted request box inside Terminal.Loop — terminal.go, L6669. Every query change ends up as EvtSearchNew — terminal.go, L8733 — which is the whole user-facing interface to the matcher.

The detail view follows one query byte-for-byte: ingestion paths on top, storage in the middle, the scoring engine and its fast paths below, and ranking plus the terminal loop on the right.

The Scoring Engine: Greedy V1 Versus Optimal V2

The file that gives fzf its character opens with a forty-line essay on its own algorithm. FuzzyMatchV1 finds the first fuzzy occurrence in O(n) with a forward scan, then walks backwards to shrink the matched window; it is fast but provably suboptimal because it never reconsiders an earlier alignment — the trade-off is spelled out at algo.go, L8. FuzzyMatchV2 implements a modified Smith-Waterman dynamic program that examines all occurrences and returns the highest-scoring one, at O(nm) cost when a match exists and O(n) when it does not — algo.go, L23.

V2 runs in four phases. Phase 1 runs a byte-level prefilter, asciiFuzzyIndex, which skips through the text with SIMD-friendly byte searches to find the narrowest window that can contain the pattern — algo.go, L420. Phase 2 computes a bonus per character position and the first DP row — algo.go, L778. Phase 3 fills the score matrix row by row, tracking gap runs and consecutive-match streaks — algo.go, L848. Phase 4 is an optional backtrace that reconstructs the exact matched positions for highlight rendering — algo.go, L920.

The scoring constants are the personality of the tool. A matched character is worth 16 points, opening a gap costs 3 and extending one costs 1, matching at a word boundary or after a slash earns 8 (the bonus is tuned to die out once the gap grows past 8 characters), camelCase humps earn 7, and consecutive streaks earn 4 — all defined together at algo.go, L112. The first pattern character gets its bonus doubled, because what you type first predicts what you want most.

Two fast paths short-circuit the general machinery. A single ASCII character never allocates a matrix; the code jumps occurrence to occurrence and stops early once it hits a boundary bonus — algo.go, L514. A two-character query collapses DP rows zero and one into scalar running state in a single fused pass — algo.go, L562. These are not heuristics: equivalence tests in algo_test.go force the general path and assert identical results, and make fuzz actively fuzzes the fast paths against the reference implementation.

Ranking: A 64-Bit Key and a Radix Sort

fzf ranks by relevance, never by recency — but the nuance is worth unpacking. The --tiebreak criteria compile into a fixed sortCriteria slice that is set once at startup and never changes — result.go, L120. When each match is built, every criterion is folded into one of four uint16 slots: score (inverted so smaller wins), whole-word chunk length, trimmed item length, and begin/end offsets — result.go, L59. The first criterion lands in the most significant slot, so “tiebreak” is really a compound primary key.

On 386/amd64/arm64, compareRanks reads those four slots as one uint64 through an unsafe pointer cast and does a single integer compare — result_x86.go, L7. Every worker sorts its own partial results with a stable LSD radix sort over that key: eight byte-passes, with any all-zero byte position skipped entirely — result.go, L354. Lists under 128 items fall back to a plain comparison sort because setup overhead dominates. The merge across workers is lazy: Merger.mergedGet advances per-list cursors and always emits the smallest remaining rank, so the user can read the first page of results before the whole merge finishes — merger.go, L155.

Where does time fit? Only after acceptance. When you multi-select items, the output order is re-sorted by the moment you picked each one, via byTimeOrder — terminal.go, L500 — so --multi output reflects your intent sequence, not the search ranking. Scheme presets reshape the criteria instead: --scheme=path ranks by score, then pathname, then length — options.go, L1342 — and fzf auto-selects that scheme when stdin is a TTY and it is walking files — options.go, L3952.

One Million Lines Without a Stutter

Ingestion is deliberately boring. The reader scans a reusable 128 KB slab, splits on newlines (or NUL bytes with --read0), and pushes each record — reader buffers and slab sizes are constants at constants.go, L16, and the split loop is reader.go, L153. With stdin a TTY and no FZF_DEFAULT_COMMAND, fzf instead walks directories in parallel through the fastwalk library — reader.go, L270. A single mutex guards the chunk list; the writer appends chunks while matchers work only on immutable snapshots, duplicated at the boundary so a mid-chunk append can never race a scan — chunklist.go, L118.

The real anti-stutter weapon is caching at two granularities. Per chunk, matching indexes are stored as bitmaps keyed by query string, and on a miss the cache hands back the longest cached prefix or suffix of the current query, so typing “foob” after “foo” only diffs the last character — cache.go, L72. Whole results are memoized too: an unchanged item count plus a repeat query returns the previous merger outright — matcher.go, L126. Both caches refuse low-selectivity queries: chunks with more than 512 matches are never bitmap-cached and mergers above 100,000 matches are never memoized — constants.go, L48.

Pattern parsing is its own mini-language: ^prefix, suffix$, 'exact, !inverse, "quoted exact", and | for OR-groups, all parsed into term sets that AND across sets and OR within — pattern.go, L168. The common case gets a dedicated bypass: a single non-inverse fuzzy term calls the algorithm function directly, skipping the generic term machinery — pattern.go, L340. Even memory churn is engineered away: every match scratch buffer comes from per-worker Slab arenas of pre-allocated int16/int32 slices, sized once — slab.go, L8 and constants.go, L44 — so steady-state searching performs close to zero allocations. It is the same allocation discipline you see in other hot Go tools like ripgrep’s mmap-heavy search loop, and it pairs beautifully with pipe sources such as fd — fd | fzf is the canonical combo — or with git output for interactive branch and stash pickers.

From Make Build to First Search

The build is refreshingly plain. BUILD.md requires only Go 1.23 or newer; make builds a binary for your platform into target/, and make install copies it to bin/ — the targets live at Makefile, L88 and Makefile, L126. The Makefile detects your architecture via uname and stamps version and revision into the binary through -ldflags "-X main.version=..." — Makefile, L37. make build hands off to goreleaser for all-platform archives — Makefile, L131.

The module is nearly dependency-free: go.mod pulls in tcell for fullscreen TUI, fastwalk for the directory walker, uniseg for Unicode segmentation, and a handful of terminal helpers. Entry is main.go, which embeds the shell key-binding scripts and man page into the binary via go:embed and then calls fzf.Run(options) — main.go, L113. From there, the pieces you now know assemble in one function: chunk list, terminal, reader goroutine, matcher loop, coordinator. The first keystroke you type lands in a system that has already been ingesting data the whole time.

Honest Limits

fzf is fast, but the source is candid about trade-offs. V2’s optimality has a cap: when the product of text and pattern length exceeds the slab capacity, or the pattern runs past 1000 runes, fzf silently falls back to greedy V1 — algo.go, L740. Scores accumulate in 16-bit slots, so extreme scores saturate rather than overflow. Queries containing inverse terms or OR-groups are excluded from chunk-scope caching — pattern.go, L115 — and a query with only inverse terms can’t be sorted at all, only filtered. The interactive UI leans on tcell as an optional fullscreen backend chosen at startup — terminal.go, L1017 — while the default LightRenderer hand-parses ANSI escape sequences; and terminal.go itself is a single file of roughly 8,400 lines, a deliberate monolith that contains the previewer, jump mode, and every action in the keymap. None of these are bugs — they are the visible edges of the same obsession: keep every keystroke cheap enough to pay for a million times per second.
entry.summary: How fzf scores a million lines per keystroke: the Smith-Waterman fuzzy matcher, 1024-item chunk storage, CPU-wide parallel search, and the terminal event loop, explained from the Go source.

entry.title: Inside Git Internals: How the Object Model, Packfiles, and Commit Walks Actually Work

link.title: Inside Git Internals: How the Object Model, Packfiles, and Commit Walks Actually Work

entry.content:
Run git status in a huge repository — say the CPython tree after its move to GitHub — and it answers instantly, while some other tools on the same machine take seconds. Run git log in two repos of comparable history and one may finish in a blink while the other churns. Nothing about your files changed; what differs is how git models what is on disk. Git is not a database of diffs or snapshots in the way most people assume — it is a content-addressed filesystem with three fast bookkeeping layers stacked on top, and nearly every command you type is a walk over that filesystem.

The evidence is sitting in .git/objects right now. Open it and you find 256 two-hex-character directories (ab/, c3/, …), each holding small zlib-compressed files named by a 40-character hash. Those files are your files — but not stored per-branch or per-commit. They are stored once, globally, keyed by the hash of their own content. Nothing inside a loose object ever mentions a branch or even a filename. That single design decision explains deduplication, cheap branches, and why git gc matters.

It also explains why clone sizes surprise people. Two repositories with a similar amount of history can unpack to very different sizes on disk, because git does not store history as a fixed format — it recomputes a compressed representation of it at pack time, using delta heuristics that depend on which objects were chosen as compression bases. Understanding git’s internals means understanding that trade-off, and the heuristics live in plain sight in the C source. This post walks the actual implementation: how object ids are computed and looked up, how the index and refs work, how delta compression squeezes a pack, and how a commit walk finds what you asked for.

Git's core as one graph: commands touch the index, write into the object database through odb_write_object_ext, resolve names through refs, decode packfiles on demand, and traverse history through the revision machinery.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • A commit is made by cmd_commit, L1696, whose real work happens in prepare_to_commit, L762: load staged state, run hooks, get a message — then write objects and move refs.
  • Every write goes through odb_write_object_ext, L696, which hashes the content first; if the object already exists, odb_freshen_object, L566 just refreshes its mtime and skips the write entirely.
  • Loose objects land at a path derived from their own hash: odb_loose_path, L60 builds objects/ab/cdef…, with the fanout directory added by fill_loose_path, L46.
  • Naming is its own subsystem: repo_get_oid, L1538 accepts hex, ref names, @{…} expressions and :path forms via get_oid_basic, L667, while repo_find_unique_abbrev_r, L585 computes the shortest prefix that stays unambiguous.
  • Refs are resolved symbolically by refs_resolve_ref_unsafe, L2136, which follows HEAD → refs/heads/master → an oid, bounded by SYMREF_MAXDEPTH.
  • The index is a single mmapped file, read by do_read_index, L2222 after verify_hdr, L1725 checks the DIRC signature and version.
  • Packed objects are decoded by unpack_entry, L1515, which walks a delta chain back to a real base while paging bytes in through use_pack, L608 — sliding mmap windows, not full-file reads.
  • Walks begin at prepare_revision_walk, L4019, which sorts tips by date, runs limit_list, L1446 to prune excluded ancestors, and applies topological order only when asked.

The detail view: from cmd_commit through hash verification and ref backends, down to delta window search in try_delta and the commit-graph-aware traversal in prepare_revision_walk.

The Object Model: Everything Is a Hash

Git’s four object types — blob, tree, commit, tag — share one storage format. To store an object, git first builds a header of the form <type> <size>\0 in format_object_header, L102, then concatenates it with the payload. The SHA-1 (or SHA-256) of those bytes is the object’s name, and that is why identical files across a million commits share a single blob: the name depends only on content.

What lands on disk is that payload, zlib-compressed, at the fanout path described above. The compression call itself is a plain git_deflate, L784 in the loose-object writer. Reading is the mirror image: check_object_signature, L113 re-hashes the decompressed bytes and compares them to the name the object was fetched under — integrity checking is free because the address is the hash.

Once loaded, every object lives in a typed in-memory representation. parse_object, L398 reads the object, verifies its hash, and dispatches to parse_object_buffer, L261, which understands each type’s grammar — trees as (mode, name, oid) triples, commits as headers plus a message. Nothing is parsed twice if it can be avoided; parsed objects are cached on the repository.

The clever part is lookup. Given git show abc123, git does not need all 40 characters — repo_get_oid, L1538 and get_oid_basic, L667 scan candidates matching the prefix and apply type hints, so an ambiguous abbreviation that could be a commit or a tag prefers the commit via disambiguate_commit_only, L138. The same logic in reverse, repo_find_unique_abbrev_r, L585, is why your short hashes occasionally grow longer: git widens them until they are unique again. The hash family itself is an abstraction (hash.h), so the object database can compute a second, compat hash during writes as visible in odb_write_object_ext, L696.

The Index and Refs: Git’s Fast Layers

The index is not a diff and not a patch — it is a flat, ordered list of (path, mode, oid, stat) records, and it is the only file git status must consult to separate “what changed” from “what is staged”. The format is documented in gitformat-index.adoc: a DIRC magic header, a version, entry count, then entries. Reads are an mmap plus a signature check (do_read_index, L2222, verify_hdr, L1725); writes serialize entries back with path compression in ce_write_entry, L2663, all under a .lock file via write_locked_index, L3384. Each entry records the file’s stat data, which is why status can trust most files without hashing them — and why touching timestamps forces a re-hash.

Refs are even cheaper. A branch is a 41-byte text file containing an oid. refs_resolve_ref_unsafe, L2136 implements the resolution loop: read the raw ref; if it starts with ref: , recurse into the pointed-to name, up to SYMREF_MAXDEPTH — that is how HEAD resolves to your branch to a commit. The generic API sits above swappable backends: the classic files backend reads loose refs and falls through to the mmapped packed-refs file (files_read_raw_ref, L657, packed_read_raw_ref, L835), while the newer reftable backend keeps refs in a log-structured, sorted table (reftable_be_read_raw_ref, L881). Updates go through refs_update_ref, L1579, which verifies the old value before swapping — the foundation of compare-and-swap semantics. Reflogs are written alongside, which is why “deleted” commits stay reachable until expiry.

Packfiles and Delta Compression

Loose objects are for small, recent history. Scale demands compression, and git’s answer is the packfile — a single append-mostly file plus a .idx index, documented in gitformat-pack.adoc. The index maps oid → offset with a binary-searchable table (find_pack_entry_one, L1815); the pack itself stores objects either whole or as deltas against other objects in the same pack.

Two kinds of delta exist: OFS_DELTA, which points backward by offset, and REF_DELTA, which names a base object. Decoding is the job of unpack_entry, L1515: it drills down through delta headers to the innermost base — consulting a small in-memory delta base cache first — then applies deltas on the way back up. Byte access goes through use_pack, L608, which hands out mmap windows and unmaps old ones behind a fixed window count, so reading a 2 GB pack never requires 2 GB of address space.

Packing is where the real money is saved, and it is heuristic. cmd_pack_objects, L5113 sorts candidate objects — by type, name-hash, and size, so similar filenames are adjacent in the window — then try_delta, L2802 diffs each candidate against neighbors until the delta stops improving, bounded by --depth and a max-size rule that rejects deltas larger than half the target. On write, existing deltas from source packs are copied verbatim when valid (write_reuse_object, L635), falling back to encoding from scratch in write_no_reuse_object, L516 when the reuse checks fail. The heuristics are explained further in pack-heuristics.adoc. This is why histories that look similar can pack differently: window contents and base selection differ per repository.

How a Commit Walk Actually Traverses

Every git log, rev-list, and merge-base computation funnels through one engine. setup_revisions, L3048 parses arguments like A..B into object flags; then prepare_revision_walk, L4019 takes the pending tips, sorts them by commit date, and chooses a strategy: if the request is “limited” — anything with exclusions or bounds — it runs limit_list, L1446, which pops commits in date order and, upon hitting an UNINTERESTING commit, floods that mark over its ancestors via mark_parents_uninteresting, L278. That flood is what makes git log main..feature terminate at the merge base instead of walking to the dawn of time.

Parsing each commit is parse_commit_buffer, L516: validate the tree line, collect every parent line, and attach them — with graft and shallow-clone substitutions applied where configured. The two orderings git offers fall out cleanly: date order needs nothing extra, while topological order is a post-pass, sort_in_topological_order, L938. The big optimization is the commit-graph file: parse_commit_in_graph, L1075 supplies parent lists and generation numbers straight from a binary index, without inflating or parsing a single commit object — which is exactly why large histories, like the Rust and TypeScript monorepos, stay fast to walk once the graph file is written.

From Clone to First Commit

Building git from source is pleasantly old-school, and the tree verifies it. The canonical instructions in INSTALL are simply make followed by make install — the top-level Makefile drives everything, with build knobs overridable via a config.mak. If you prefer autoconf, make configure regenerates the ./configure script from configure.ac, then ./configure --prefix=/usr && make all doc produces binaries and man pages. There is also a second build system: meson.build is present and documented in build-systems.adoc, and a profile-feedback build (make profile) exists that rebuilds git after running the test suite as training data — the INSTALL notes it buys a few percent on CPU-bound work at the cost of building twice.

You can run the freshly built git without installing: the build tree ships bin-wrappers/, and INSTALL documents prepending it to PATH. First commit is then git commit through the very code path traced above. Notably, the tree now also contains contrib/libgit-rs — early Rust bindings — showing the project slowly exposing its object database beyond C.

Honest Limits

The object model is stable but the hash beneath it is not final. The migration plan from SHA-1 lives in hash-function-transition.adoc: since v2.13.0 git ships a hardened SHA-1 (collision detection, vendored under sha1collisiondetection/), but SHA-1 remains the default algorithm, and the transition is implemented as plumbing — the compat-algo hashing visible in odb_write_object_ext, L696 — rather than a done deal. Repositories like Go that moved hosting around have felt similar storage-format transitions; git’s is still in progress.

Delta compression is also heuristic, not optimal: the window/depth bounds in try_delta, L2802 trade pack size for CPU, and the design doc admits the search is approximate. The index’s stat-based freshness means it can mark clean files dirty after timestamp churn (the racy-git problem, described in racy-git.adoc). And the ref layer is in mid-migration too: files, packed-refs, and reftable backends all coexist, selected per-repository. Finally, the commit-graph is strictly an accelerator — parse_commit_in_graph, L1075 only applies when the file exists and covers your commits; without it, walks inflate every commit object the old way.
entry.summary: How git really stores your history: content-addressed objects, the index, refs and reflogs, packfile delta compression, and commit graph walks — with line-level links into git's C source.

entry.title: Inside Neovim: How the RPC Core and Lua Host Actually Work

link.title: Inside Neovim: How the RPC Core and Lua Host Actually Work

entry.content:
Run nvim --headless +'lua print(vim.api.nvim_buf_line_count(0))' +qa on a file and you get an answer with no window, no terminal, no user. That is a strange property for an editor: the same binary you use interactively is also a scriptable service that speaks a binary protocol. It works because Neovim was restructured into something Vim never was — an event-loop core with an API surface, rather than a tangle of modal code with scripts bolted on.

The second oddity shows up in plugin behavior. Vimscript execution was famously blocking: call a job, wait, freeze the UI. In Neovim, plugins fire timers, watch jobs, and react to RPC notifications without the editor ever stalling. That is not magic either — it falls out of one design decision: everything, including your plugin callbacks, runs as events on a single libuv loop that the editor itself lives on.

So what actually happens between :lua vim.api.nvim_buf_set_lines(0, 0, 1, false, {"x"}) and a buffer changing on screen? This post walks the C source of src/nvim on master and traces that path end to end: bootstrap, the loop, the msgpack channel, the two scripting hosts, the buffer data model, and the redraw pass. Every symbol and line anchor below was verified against the tree.

Neovim from boot to redraw: the libuv loop, the msgpack-RPC channel, the two scripting hosts, the buffer data model, and the UI layer. Rendered from src/nvim on master.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Bootstrap is a strict sequence: main, L255 parses argv, runs early_init, L193 for the first option pass, then calls event_init, L158 at L284 to bring up the loop before any UI or user config exists.
  • There is exactly one loop object: the global Loop main_loop, L146, initialized by loop_init(&main_loop) at L160. Input, jobs, timers, signals, and RPC all multiplex through it.
  • Waiting is bounded: loop_poll_events, L78 delegates to loop_uv_run, L41, which invokes libuv uv_run at L59 in UV_RUN_ONCE mode — process one batch of I/O, then return so queued work executes promptly.
  • Events queue up through multiqueue_put_event, L134 into queues built by multiqueue_new, L86; child queues from multiqueue_new_child, L92, like the resize_events queue created at L162, flush along with their parent.
  • Remote clients attach because server_init, L35 binds --listen addresses; each accepted channel flips to RPC mode in rpc_start, L80, and decoded requests land in handle_request, L322.
  • One request can drive either scripting host: nvim_eval/nvim_exec2 from vimscript.c, L152, or nvim_exec_lua, whose real entry is nlua_exec, L1721 in the Lua host.
  • Buffer edits from any client go through nvim_buf_set_lines, L326, which splices lines, re-anchors extmarks via extmark_splice at L447, notifies watchers with changed_lines at L451, and repairs cursors with fix_cursor at L455.
  • Redraw is two-phase: redraw_all_later, L2715 only flags work, and the single pass update_screen, L483 turns flags into grid events that attached UIs consume.

The Event Loop That Runs Everything

Neovim’s core claim to modularity is that the editor and your plugins share one scheduler. event_init wires main_loop, and from then on every subsystem registers libuv handles on it: streams for channels, processes for :terminal and jobstart, timers for delayed work, signal watchers for SIGWINCH. When main() finishes bootstrapping, it settles into polling this loop and processing queues until teardown.

The mechanics matter. loop_poll_events, L78 takes a timeout in milliseconds, runs UV_RUN_ONCE, and then drains the queue that pairs with it. Because each poll handles at most one I/O batch before yielding to queued callbacks, no single subsystem can starve the others indefinitely — the editor interleaves RPC traffic, key handling, and redraw work in small slices. Events themselves are tiny structs: a function pointer plus an argument, appended with multiqueue_put_event, L134 and invoked when their queue is processed. Child queues matter for correctness: resize_events exists precisely so resize handling can be prioritized relative to the parent queue instead of being interleaved arbitrarily.

This loop is also why :terminal is honest about what it is — a real PTY child process streaming through the same loop, so an interactive shell such as fish runs in a split pane with the editor never blocking on it. If you know how event loops power language runtimes, the shape will feel familiar; it is the same idea Neovim imported, in C, with libuv.

msgpack-RPC: How Clients Talk to the Core

The API surface is reachable from inside (vim.api) and from outside over msgpack-RPC, and both paths converge on the same dispatch. Outbound-facing, server_init, L35 accepts --listen addresses (pipes and TCP sockets). When a client connects, rpc_start, L80 marks the channel as RPC and registers its read stream. Bytes are incrementally decoded by the msgpack unpacker (src/nvim/msgpack_rpc/unpacker.c), which emits either requests or notifications; requests carry a message id so the response, encoded by src/nvim/msgpack_rpc/packer.c, can be correlated.

handle_request, L322 resolves the method name to the generated handler for it — the same handlers vim.api calls in-process. That is the whole trick behind ecosystem tooling: an LSP client, a GUI, a test harness, or a plugin host built on Node all speak to identical API functions (nvim_eval at L152, nvim_exec2 at L54, and so on). Nothing about “remote” changes semantics.

One rule trips up new plugin authors: handlers that run as events on the loop may execute in a fast context where blocking calls are forbidden. Lua can detect this with nlua_in_fast_event, L1300, and the vim.call bridge nlua_call, L1317 actively rejects deferred-unsafe Vimscript functions with a hard error rather than deadlocking. This is why async plugins use vim.schedule/vim.defer_fn to hop back onto a safe queue slot — the guard rail lives right there in the bridge.

Hosting Lua and Vimscript Side by Side

Two interpreters share one process. The Vimscript evaluator is classic C: eval_expr, L594 parses an expression into a typval_T, descending through eval1, L1915 — a recursive-descent grammar whose atom level is eval7, L2650. Compound assignment operators like += route through eexe_mod_op, L201. Values stay in Vimscript’s own type system all the way down.

The Lua host is a different beast: a lua_State (global_lstate) embedded in the C process. Executing a chunk is three steps in nlua_exec, L1721: compile with luaL_loadbuffer at L1728, push the arguments as API Objects, and run under nlua_pcall, L330, which converts Lua errors into proper API errors instead of unwinding the editor. Values cross the boundary through conversion glue in src/nvim/lua/converter.c; buffers, windows, and tabpages surface in Lua as thin integer handles that call straight back into the API layer.

The bridges run both ways, which is what makes the dual-host model coherent. Vimscript reaches Lua via luaeval() and v:lua; Lua reaches Vimscript via vim.call/vim.fn through nlua_call. And the crossover is not just for callers: you can write a whole module in Lua and have Vimscript invoke it — nlua_call_typval, L1758 synthesizes a require('module').func(...) call with typval_T arguments, and Lua-implemented user commands execute through nlua_do_ucmd, L2405. The callable-bridging variant nlua_exec_typval_callable, L1691 handles calling a Lua function reference directly from Vimscript code. If you have ever embedded an interpreter in C — the way CPython embeds into C extensions — the pattern is the same; Neovim just applies it to a live editor instead of a REPL.

Buffers, Windows, and Change Propagation

The data model has three anchors. buf_T from buflist_new, L1984 is the text container; its contents live in memline structures, opened by open_buffer, L250 — whose comment is refreshingly literal: “open the memfile and read the file into memory.” Lazy loading exists too: buf_ensure_loaded, L222 opens the buffer only when needed, at L236. Windows (win_T) and tab pages are laid out by window.c, starting from win_alloc_first, L4345; a window never owns text, it views a buffer, which is why splits are cheap and why cursor repair after edits is per-window.

That repair step is visible right inside the API edit path. nvim_buf_set_lines performs a precise sequence: splice the requested line range, then extmark_splice, L447 re-anchors extmarks so decorations, LSP diagnostics, and plugin marks survive the edit with their semantics intact; changed_lines, L451 notifies every attached watcher — including remote RPC clients subscribed via nvim_buf_attach; and fix_cursor, L455 adjusts cursor positions in the affected windows. Editor events fire alongside: apply_autocmds, L1375 is the general entry for firing autocommand groups, and the grouped variant at L1481 does the matching work.

Redraw closes the loop. Editing code flags the screen via redraw_all_later, L2715 — it does not draw. The actual pass, update_screen, L483, runs later on the loop and turns accumulated flags into grid-level events. Because the UI layer (src/nvim/ui.c) abstracts the client protocol — ui_refresh, L189 reconciles which UI capabilities are active and pushes ui_call_option_set at L217 — the same core can serve the built-in TUI and external clients like a GUI or a GPU terminal such as alacritty. Scheduling respects the loop: ui_schedule_refresh, L288 puts a refresh event on resize_events with multiqueue_put at L290, so even redraw scheduling goes through the queue machinery rather than redrawing inline.

From Make Build to First Buffer

Building from source is deliberately boring. The repo uses CMake as its build system; BUILD.md documents the canonical steps: run make CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, and INSTALL.md shows installing with make install (optionally with CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX, or plain sudo make install). You do not hand-install the tricky dependencies — libuv, LuaJIT, tree-sitter and friends are fetched automatically into .deps/ by the deps build. Ninja is not required but is picked up automatically if present, which the docs recommend for faster builds. Building “PUC Lua” instead of LuaJIT is a supported variant via -DPREFER_LUA=ON, confirming LuaJIT is the default runtime, not a hard requirement.

Trace what happens when that freshly built binary starts: main() bootstraps options, event_init starts the loop, UI attaches, and the first buffer for your file materializes through open_buffer — memfile allocated, file read. From there the loop owns everything until +qa tears it down. That is the entire architecture in one breath: loop first, editor as events on the loop.

Honest Limits

The source is candid about its boundaries. The editor core — evaluator, buffer internals, redraw — is still C, and large C at that: eval.c is several thousand lines (eval_call_provider, L6602 sits near the end), drawscreen.c passes 2,700 lines, and main.c mixes CLI parsing with boot logic past the 2,000-line mark (do_user_initialization, L2131). Lua hosts the runtime layer (runtime/lua/vim/...) and calls into C through the API; it does not replace the C internals.

Vim9 script is not part of Neovim, and the tree says so directly: the lone Vim9 reference in src/nvim/runtime.c at L2728 is a comment noting Vim9 autoload is “not applicable to Nvim.” Neovim’s scripting story remains legacy Vimscript plus Lua, with Lua positioned as the forward path.

Also worth stating plainly: RPC requests execute on the main loop, single-threaded with the editor — the fast-context guards exist precisely because there is no worker thread to hide blocking calls in. And line anchors here are pinned to master on the date of this post; C files this active will drift.
entry.summary: How Neovim's libuv event loop, msgpack-RPC core, and embedded Lua host actually work, explained from src/nvim with pinned line anchors.

entry.title: Inside ripgrep: The Crate Architecture That Makes Search This Fast

link.title: Inside ripgrep: The Crate Architecture That Makes Search This Fast

entry.content:
You type rg 'fn walk_builder' in a checkout of ripgrep itself and the answer is on screen before your finger has left the Enter key. Run grep -r 'fn walk_builder' . on the same tree and you can hear the disk working: grep happily descends into target/, .git/, and every generated artifact your .gitignore exists to forget about. The speed gap is not one clever trick. It is a stack of small decisions — skip the right files, search the right way, use the right engine — wired together by an unusually disciplined crate architecture.

And ripgrep is honest about the second thing people notice: it respects .gitignore without being asked, skips hidden files and binary blobs, and still manages to be the fastest line-oriented searcher most of us have used. That combination sounds contradictory — filtering is work, and work costs time — until you read the source and see that every filter pays for itself by deleting future work.

This post walks that architecture in the actual tree (ripgrep 15.2.0, master). Between the moment you press Enter on rg pattern and the moment matches appear, roughly ten crates cooperate: a CLI front-end parses flags, a parallel walker streams candidate files while honoring gitignore rules, a layered regex engine stack matches text, and printers format the results. Two diagrams anchor the tour — an overview you can read left to right, and a detail graph for the internals. Every link below points at a real file and line in the upstream repository.

The full path of a single rg invocation: flags become a HiArgs config, the parallel walker yields gitignore-aware haystacks, the Searcher applies the regex engine to each one, and printers sink the matches. Left to right is the life of one search.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The driver is thin on purpose. run, L77 dispatches by mode: single-threaded search when -j 1, otherwise search_parallel — which never spawns threads itself; it just feeds a visitor closure to the walker at search_parallel, L175.
  • Flags become factories. walk_builder, L874 in HiArgs turns CLI options into a configured WalkBuilder, wiring -g globs, -t types, and the custom .rgignore filename.
  • The walker is the concurrency engine. WalkParallel::run, L1430 executes traversal on a worker pool whose size defaults to min(ncpu, 12) at threads, L1539 — parallelism sits exactly where the filesystem syscalls are.
  • Gitignore state is persistent. Ignore, L94 links each directory’s compiled matchers to its parent’s, so descending the tree never re-parses an ignore file.
  • Globs never match one by one. GlobSetMatchStrategy, L685 dispatches an entire set of patterns to specialized literal, extension, prefix/suffix or regex strategies in a single pass.
  • The engine probes with literals first. RegexMatcher, L367 bundles the full regex with an optional fast_line_regex — a cheaper matcher that never misses but may false-positive — used at find_candidate_line, L490.
  • Each file gets a strategy. search_path, L643 opens the haystack and tries a memory map first at mmap, L689, falling back to buffered streaming.
  • The hot loop is line-shaped. match_by_line_fast, L385 jumps straight to the next candidate match and sinks whole lines — no per-line allocation on the fast path.

The detail view: how flags become matchers, how the Ignore chain layers .gitignore/.ignore/.rgignore through GlobSet, how ConfiguredHIR compiles the engine, and where the 64 KB line buffer feeds the fast match loop.

A Workspace, Not a Monolith

The root Cargo.toml defines a single binary target — name = "rg" with path = "crates/core/main.rs" — plus nine workspace libraries: globset, grep, cli, matcher, pcre2, printer, regex, searcher, and ignore. crates/core is the only place that knows about a terminal; everything else is a plain library with a narrow job. matcher holds just the engine-agnostic Matcher trait, globset knows nothing about gitignore semantics, and the grep facade crate exists only to re-export the others under one name.

This shape has a practical payoff: the internals are reusable. Any tool can take the walker, the searcher and a matcher and assemble its own search command without inheriting a single CLI flag. It also keeps the crates individually benchmarkable — when a regression appears, the layer that caused it is visible in the structure, not buried in a 10,000-line main.rs. The workspace builds against Rust edition 2024 with a pinned rust-version of 1.96, which matters because the crates lean on recent regex-crate APIs. If you have read our Rust compiler source tour, this is the same workspace philosophy that the language’s own repo uses: many small crates, one thin binary shell.

The Regex Engine Stack: Literals Before Regex

When HiArgs::matcher() builds a matcher, the default path is grep-regex. Patterns are parsed into a ConfiguredHIR — an AST translated to a HIR that still remembers its configuration — and then compiled by to_regex with limits tuned for a CLI: a 10 MB one-pass DFA cap, a 1 MB full-DFA cap, and a 1,000-state limit. A pathological pattern fails to compile instead of hanging the search.

The interesting part is what wraps the compiled regex. RegexMatcher holds three fields: the real regex, an optional fast_line_regex, and a set of bytes that can never appear in a match. The fast regex is extracted from the pattern’s literals — for alternations like cat|dog|bird, it is just the alternation of those literals, which the underlying engine can match with memchr-class speed. During the line loop, find_candidate_line runs the probe first; only lines that survive go through the full regex. With -F/--fixed-strings, the builder skips regex parsing entirely and assembles the HIR from the literal bytes themselves. PCRE2 is optional behind the pcre2 feature: the PatternMatcher enum holds either a Rust regex or a PCRE2 matcher, -P selects it, and on 64-bit targets the builder enables the PCRE2 JIT with a 10 MB stack.

The Walker: Parallelism Where the Filesystem Is

ripgrep does not use a thread-pool crate. WalkParallel::run hands directories around a hand-rolled Message::Work/Quit loop — closer to the channel idioms you would write by hand in Go than to a generic scheduler. Each visitor callback runs on a worker thread that owns a clone of the SearchWorker, so searching is shared-nothing except for the output buffer.

Correctness lives in the Ignore chain. Every directory gets an IgnoreInner carrying matchers for custom ignore files, .ignore, .gitignore, and .git/info/exclude, plus a has_git flag. matched_ignore walks the parent chain and applies them in git’s precedence order, gated by require_git so gitignore rules only apply inside repositories. Each Gitignore wraps a GlobSet; matched strips the directory prefix and queries it with a reusable match pool. The semantics intentionally mirror git’s own implementation of these files — negations, directory-only patterns, anchoring — so a file git ignores is a file ripgrep skips, without shelling out to git.

Glob matching itself is where globset earns its keep. A GlobSet compiles its patterns once and dispatches on GlobSetMatchStrategy: exact literals go into a hash map guarded by a 64-bit length bitmap, basename literals match only the file name, and extension/prefix/suffix strategies cover the shapes gitignore files actually contain. Only genuinely regex-shaped globs fall back to a RegexSet, and even then a required-extension prefilter can reject a candidate before any pattern runs.
